functional_compartments.name: Lumbricals 1-2 (radial)
functional_compartments.function_note: Unipennate-origin, unusual among skeletal muscles for originating from a tendon (FDP) rather than a bone; median-nerve innervated, unlike lumbricals 3-4.

functional_compartments.function_note: Documented ulnar-nerve innervation, distinct from lumbricals 1-2 -- the same radial/ulnar innervation split pattern seen in the foot's lumbricals.

ultrasound_injection_approach.transducer_placement: Transverse on the palm below the thenar eminence, at the midpoint of the metacarpals of digits II-V. For injection, about 1 cm proximal to the metacarpophalangeal joints.
ultrasound_injection_approach.depth_layer: Palmar, with the palmar interossei deeper between the metacarpal cortices.
ultrasound_injection_approach.identification_cues: Distinctly oval. Working radial to ulnar the sequence is L1 with FDS2 and FDP2, then L2 with FDS3 and FDP3, and so on.
ultrasound_injection_approach.source: Diaconu S et al. (Elias University Hospital), 'A Visual Guide to Ultrasound-Guided Botulinum Toxin Injection in Spasticity: Part I -- Distal Upper Limb Muscles', Toxins 17(3):107 (2025), doi:10.3390/toxins17030107

trigger_points.location_description: Lumbrical I, in its lumbrical canal on the radial side of the index finger flexor digitorum profundus tendon; palpated deep in the palm alongside the flexor tendons, between the 2nd and 3rd metacarpals.
trigger_points.referred_pain_pattern: Projects along the radial side of the index finger, with deep palm ache between the metacarpals -- the same rule that governs the interossei of the same ray.
trigger_points.activation_perpetuating_factors: High-repetition fine flexion (keyboard, piano and string instruments, writing, sewing, tweezers/laparoscopic instruments), sustained hook grip; splinting in the intrinsic-plus position.
trigger_points.notes: Lumbrical overuse can crowd the flexed-fist carpal tunnel and contribute to nocturnal CTS symptoms -- both the tunnel and the muscle pattern may need treatment. Needling here must respect the digital neurovascular bundle travelling with the muscle in its canal, and the superficial palmar arch proximally.
trigger_points.source: Simons, Travell & Simons Trigger Point Manual, Vol. 1, Ch. 40, pp. 786-793 -- as cited in this atlas's uploaded hand intrinsic muscle reference document

clinical.compiled_by: repository owner (physician); hand_intrinsic_muscles_reference_v1.html, compiled 03/09/2026. Source hierarchy used. (1) Peer-reviewed anatomical and biomechanical studies (bibliographic data and abstracts retrieved via PubMed/NCBI, 01–03/09/2026; DOIs linked in the reference list); (2) reference textbooks — Standring (Gray's Anatomy, 42nd ed., 2021), Kapandji (2007), Green's Operative Hand Surgery (8th ed., 2022), Brand & Hollister (1999); (3) Simons, Travell & Simons, The Trigger Point Manual Vol. 1, 2nd ed. (1999) and 3rd ed. (2019) for trigger-point (TrP) referral patterns; (4) StatPearls/NCBI Bookshelf for cross-checking. No item below relies on blogs or unattributed aggregators; where secondary TrP summaries were used to confirm Travell & Simons figures, they are graded accordingly in the verification table.
clinical.function_biomechanics: MCP flexion with PIP+DIP extension — the intrinsic-plus posture — but their genius is the linkage: the only muscles running from a flexor tendon to the extensor apparatus, so contraction simultaneously pulls the extensor hood proximally and drags the FDP tendon distally, unloading its passive tension across the IP joints — the muscle that "relaxes its own antagonist", plus a small but significant MCP flexion/radial-deviation moment [17]. Architecture matches the job: fibre length ≈ 85–90% of muscle length (extreme excursion design) with the smallest PCSA in the upper limb, ~1/10–1/20 of FDP — force is not their business [6][37]. They are extraordinarily spindle-rich, the prototype of small "kinesiological monitor" muscles that provide proprioceptive feedback while a large parallel muscle does the work — here, sensing the rate of hand closure during grasp [17][18]. Clinical corollaries: the lumbrical-plus finger (paradoxical IP extension on grasp when FDP is divided distal to the lumbrical origin, after mid-phalanx amputation or an over-long tendon graft) [19]; lumbrical/interosseous tightness on the Bunnell test after trauma or spasticity [35]; and their contribution to grip loss after median block (−32%) [7].
clinical.adjacent_structures: Relations · fascia · spaces · closed sacs: Each runs in its lumbrical canal (septa of the palmar aponeurosis) with the digital neurovascular bundle — an infection highway from web space to thenar (L-I) and midpalmar (L-II–IV) spaces [1][2][32]. Because the origin rides on the FDP tendon, it is mobile: in full finger extension the lumbrical bellies sit ~8 mm distal to the carpal tunnel, and with a full fist they travel ~30 mm into the tunnel [8]; with lumbricals intact, carpal-tunnel pressure climbs progressively with finger flexion and stays flat once they are excised [9]. That is the anatomical engine of grip-related ("dynamic"/occupational) CTS and of the hypertrophied or proximally originating lumbrical variants seen at release [3][8][9]. The distal margin of the ulnar bursa surrounds their origins.

trigger_points.activation_perpetuating_factors: high-repetition fine flexion — keyboard, piano and string instruments, writing, sewing, tweezers/laparoscopic instruments, sustained hook grip; splinting in intrinsic-plus. Palpation is through the palm between the metacarpals (deep, alongside the flexor tendons); needling here must respect the digital neurovascular bundle travelling with the muscle in its canal and the superficial arch proximally [1][24]. A practical loop to remember: lumbrical overuse → fist-loaded tunnel crowding → nocturnal CTS symptoms — treat both the tunnel and the muscle pattern [8][9][30].

Baltimore: Williams & Wilkins; 1999 — Ch. 39 (adductor & opponens pollicis), Ch. 40 (interossei, lumbricals, abductor digiti minimi; pp. 786-793).

pain_referred_into_this_muscle_from: Myofascial: FDS/FDP (lancinating volar digit pain — the classic "finger" muscles), extensor digitorum (dorsal digit), interossei of the same ray, scalenes (index), pectoralis minor/latissimus (ring–little), palmaris longus (superficial palm) [24].
Non-myofascial: trigger finger (A1), MCP/PIP synovitis and osteoarthritis, digital-nerve lesions, C7–C8 roots, Dupuytren cords (contracture, usually painless) [35].
clinical.caveat: Most myofascial hand pain is imported: shoulder-girdle, arm and forearm TrPs project distally far more often than intrinsic TrPs project proximally. Patterns below are the prototype maps of Simons, Travell & Simons (Vol. 1, 2nd ed., 1999; 3rd ed., 2019) — screening guides, not fingerprints; individual spread is wide [24][25]. Non-myofascial mimics are listed per zone for the same working position [5][29][31][35]. TrP → = habitual referred-pain direction of that muscle's trigger points (Simons, Travell & Simons 1999/2019); patterns are prototypes — individual variation is wide.
